items.stem: Why is enterprise value distinct from equity value?

options.text: Enterprise value is the value of the operating business before net debt; equity value deducts net debt
options.rationale: Correct: equity value = enterprise value - net debt (plus/minus adjustments).

options.text: They are the same number expressed differently
options.rationale: They differ by net debt and other items.
Net debt usually makes equity value smaller.

options.text: Enterprise value ignores the business's cash flows
options.rationale: Enterprise value is driven by operating cash flows.

items.explanation: Correct: enterprise value is pre-net-debt; equity value deducts net debt.

items.stem: Which TWO are valid ways to estimate terminal value in a DCF? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Gordon growth (perpetuity) on a normalised final-year cash flow
options.rationale: Correct: the perpetuity-growth method is standard.

options.text: An exit multiple applied to a final-year metric
options.rationale: Correct: the exit-multiple method is standard and worth cross-checking.
History does not set terminal value.

options.text: Using the current share price as terminal value
options.rationale: That is circular and not a terminal-value method.

items.explanation: Correct: Gordon growth and an exit multiple are the two standard, cross-checkable methods.

items.stem: A peer set for trading comparables should be selected mainly on the basis of:

options.text: Similar business model, growth and risk profile
options.rationale: Correct: true comparability is about economics, not just industry label.

options.text: Being the largest companies you can find
options.rationale: Size alone does not make a peer comparable.

options.text: Sharing the first letter of the company name

options.rationale: Choosing high multiples biases the valuation.

items.explanation: Correct: comparables must match business model, growth and risk, not just the sector.
